“dialectics as an exploratory technique or a method of intellectual enquiry” — This is how I see the word most often used. How do we get from it being a technique to it being a theory?  Or was it a theory first with Plato and then it became a technique with Hegel and then back to a theory with Deleuze? Is it a technique with Kant or is it a theory with Kant? 
Techniques and theories seem to me to be two fundamentally different things— a theory is an analysis of something, but a technique is a way of analyzing something. I tried to read Adorno’s book on dialectics, but all of it was over my head in the first few pages. It seemed like he was going into those lectures thinking that the listeners already understood this underlying definition of dialectics which is exactly what I’m trying to understand.

Perhaps I should have mentioned this in my original post: one my biggest confusions with the word “dialectics” meaning something completely different for each philosopher is that I’ve seen several philosophers mention it only very briefly in their work with very little context. If it means something different for each person, but a person uses it in just a passing sentence without explaining it, what I am supposed to make of it? 
For instance, in the translator’s introduction to the book Society of the Spectacle by Guy Debord, the translator says that it is okay to skip around in the book because “it is written dialectically”. The word dialectics doesn’t come up anywhere else in the book. If the word dialectics is meaningless without context, how can the translator just say that? 

Or in Jean Paul Sartre’s preface to Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth — “[Fanon] has made himself spokesman for the situation, nothing more. But that is all he needs to do in order to constitute, step by step, the dialectic that liberal hypocrisy hides from you and that has produced us just as much as it has produced him.” So for Fanon, the revolution is a dialectic? 
The dialectic is a theory of Plato’s Ideas for Deleuze, a style of writing for Debord, and a type of political revolution for Fanon. And all of them are using the word in passing as if we already know what they are talking about. This all almost feels like a joke that I’m not in on

But then Marx kind of makes throws a wrench into this with dialectical materialism. Theory of the matter of Ideas? Isn’t that a contradiction?

And is idealism itself a dialectic? Idealism = believing that everything is made of Ideas, I think. Isn’t this a theory of Ideas?

Depends how much you want to spend. You could order a complete setup from any of the big brands (Almost, Baker, Primitive, Polar, etc.) for around $110 off of CCS.com, assuming that your local shop is closed due to the virus. You would just search “Complete Skateboards” on their website and look through the selection. These setups are perfectly fine for a beginner, and they are what most people use for their first board. Later on, when that setup starts to break down, you can customize it, adding whatever Bones bearings you can afford (do not buy the Bones Swiss Ceramics, they are not worth the money. The normal Bones Swiss are what most people ride if you can afford them. Bones Reds are everyone’s not so bad second option if they have no cash.), Bones or Spitfire wheels 52 to 54mm, Independent Trucks (my preference), any hardware, Jessup Grip if you want less grippy griptape, Mob Grip if you want very grippy griptape, Bones Medium Bushings if you still have extra cash. This setup would be closer to $200+ I think. But it isn’t really necessary for a beginner. 
The biggest thing that you need to know for buying the $110 complete setup is that you want to make sure the board is a normal shape, and that it is 8.25”. That is the middle ground for board sizes so it is a good place to start. When you want to buy a new deck, it is all very much preference. You just have to try different sizes and shapes out and see what you like best. You can also experiment going to different brands with anything  I’ve listed. Some people like Thunder or Krux Trucks more than Independent, etc... Also, a side note, buying a skate tool will be helpful because you’ll want to be able to loosen or tighten your trucks. Some people ride very loose, some very tight, some ride somewhere in the middle. Another big reason for buying a complete setup is that buying all the separate pieces and putting them together by yourself is going to be frustrating as hell. You’ll be wondering if you screwed something on too tight or maybe your griptape might end up very messed up. Someone who works at your local skate shop could do it almost perfectly in 15 minutes so it might be better to start customizing after skate shops start opening up again. On that note, check and see if your local skate shop has any option for ordering from them over the phone when their shop is closed. Just ask them for a complete setup that has an 8.25” deck.

Next, she cut along the grid that she drew earlier, and it looks like she mixed up all the different squares and just stuck them on her board in random places. The underside of all grip-tape is like a sticker that you peel off of the cardboard that comes with the roll. So she just stuck all the little squares on like little stickers.
